idiom_name: forwarder (checks an enable flag, then forwards) + gate (holds and flips the flag) kept by the grantor
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the target, create the enable state and a gate that can flip it, and create one forwarder that implements the target's interface. Hand the collaborator only the forwarder; keep the gate - and every other reference to the target - with the grantor. Every forwarded call must check the enable state and either forward or deny; nothing in the structure makes the target unreachable, so any alias that escapes limits what revocation can achieve. To be correct under concurrency the check and the forward must be one uninterruptible step: read the flag and forward inside the same handler (the cited repair folds the flag into the forwarding gate for exactly this reason) instead of reading the state as a separate call whose answer can go stale. State the in-flight policy explicitly: either revocation denies calls that have not yet passed the check and lets those already past it finish, or revocation drains (waits for calls in flight) using an exclusive lock. Keep the forwarder from returning or describing the target, make revocation one-way unless re-enabling is a deliberate feature, and release the wrapper when the grant ends.
code_sketch:
grant(target):
    state = EnableSlot(true)              # or fold the flag into the gate
    fwd   = Forwarder(target, state)      # per member: if !state.enabled(): deny; else target.m(...)
    gate  = Gate(state)                   # gate.flip() is the revocation event
    keep(gate); give(collaborator, fwd)   # never give(collaborator, target)
revoke: gate.flip()                       # atomic with the forward in the repaired form
pitfalls: Checking the enable state and forwarding as two separate steps (or reading the state across an asynchronous boundary) reintroduces the check-then-forward race in which a call crosses after revocation.
A forwarder that also returns the target - through a self-returning method, an unwrapped accessor, debug output or reflection - hands the collaborator an unrevokable route to the protected object.
Handing out one shared forwarder for many grants makes revocation all-or-nothing, while handing the gate to the collaborator makes revocation cooperative.

Wrong move: delete the target or endpoint to revoke one grant -> unrelated holders break while cached or queued calls may still behave differently -> instead flip a private per-grant gate and keep target lifetime separate.

Wrong move: treat task cancellation or token expiry as complete object revocation -> a cancelled task or cached credential can retain a usable capability and in-flight work can continue -> instead revoke the wrapper gate, then separately cancel or drain work.

Wrong move: share one forwarder or revocation gate across tenants -> one tenant's withdrawal becomes all-or-nothing or couples unrelated grants -> instead issue one wrapper and one private revoker for each grant.
